draft.title: FamilyBench: Testing Local LLMs on Large, Complex Family Trees—Insights and Open Questions
draft.body: FamilyBench is an open-source benchmark designed to challenge LLMs with complex, tree-like family relationships across very large contexts—up to 400 individuals over 10 generations, roughly 18k tokens. It generates synthetic family trees via Python scripts and formulates 200 questions per test, aiming to probe relational and contextual reasoning beyond typical text tasks. Initial tests on seven models (mostly open weights) show a wide range of accuracy, with Gemini 2.5 Pro scoring highest at about 81%, while others achieved lower scores and some exhibited ‘no response’ failures when token limits were exceeded. These results were obtained under fixed conditions (8k max tokens, temperature 0.3, low reasoning effort) and should be viewed as preliminary. Given the benchmark’s novelty and synthetic nature, how might we interpret these accuracy differences? Could tuning parameters or expanding question types reveal more about local LLMs’ strengths and weaknesses in handling intricate relational data? Also, what approaches might help reduce the no response rate linked to token exhaustion? I’m interested in hearing if anyone has experimented further with FamilyBench or similar large-context relational benchmarks to better understand local LLM reasoning limits.

draft.title: Insights from FamilyBench’s First Round: How Well Can Local LLMs Handle Complex Family Trees?
draft.body: FamilyBench offers an open-source benchmark focused on testing LLMs’ ability to understand and reason over complex family trees spanning large contexts—up to 400 people over 10 generations. The benchmark uses a Python tool to generate trees and 200 related questions per run. Early results from seven models show varied accuracy, with Gemini 2.5 Pro reaching over 81% accuracy and no failures to respond, whereas others had lower accuracy and some no responses attributed to token limit exhaustion. Tests were done with fixed parameters (8k max tokens, low reasoning effort, temperature 0.3), so it’s unclear how much tuning might affect outcomes. Considering these caveats, how useful do you find FamilyBench for assessing local LLMs’ relational reasoning? Are there ways to extend or complement this benchmark to better capture model capabilities or failure modes, especially regarding large context handling and complex tree-like data?

draft.title: How well does FamilyBench test LLMs on complex family tree reasoning?
draft.body:
FamilyBench proposes a unique approach to evaluating language models by generating intricate family trees and then posing questions about their relationships. This method aims to assess a model’s ability to understand and reason over complex, tree-like structures within a large context. The benchmark uses a Python program to create these trees and formulate related questions, which seems promising for testing relational comprehension beyond typical text tasks.

However, since the initial report dates from mid-2025 and comes from a single source without independent verification, it’s unclear how robust or generalizable the results are. Also, the benchmark’s reliance on synthetic data raises questions about how well models trained on natural language handle these structured challenges.

Has anyone experimented with FamilyBench or similar synthetic relational benchmarks to see if they reveal weaknesses or strengths in local LLMs that aren’t obvious from standard tests?
